title: The private slang musicians spoke
summary: Goodwin says Hayes's band deliberately used an invented language; Lovett started it, and 'accomplished' meant a woman.

story.theme_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band monikers
story.community_name: How I got my name: nicknames and band names

blocks.x: Well, I don't know. Of course these things will change and what we're doing is going to go on, we hope, for a long, long time. We can't possibly cover all the questions on this outline, this excellent outline I will repeat, prepared by Mr. Taylor.

I'm going to ask a question and this I guess will be the last one unless either one of you have something to add. Did musicians -- I guess -- they keep talking in the past on this thing, we won't talk about today -- but did musicians tend to talk about everyday matters; food, drink, lodging I suppose, chicks and whatever, in a manner that might not be understood by the average person and if so, how? This is going back, say, in the '20s and '30s.
A number of things --
All right Crook. Crook.
A number of things I can say like the band, Thamon Hayes' band, well we had a way of talking so nobody could understand but the guys who belonged to the band.
You didn't do this deliberately, it just evolved?
Yes, we did it deliberately.
Why.
Because -- so the outsider wouldn't know what we were talking about.
When you're talking about outsider, you mean a non-musician?
That's right.
A non-musician?
That's right.
Can you give us some examples?
Well, we just made up language, you know.
Do you remember that, Baby?
Yeah, well we used to say chick, you remember.
Well what I'm talking about is things we used to say like being accomplished, you wouldn't know what
we were talking about.
No.
Being accomplished?
That's a woman.
See, we were saying, 'Look at that lady', being accomplished, see.
The language sounds Italian to me.
Well this is the thing we made up ourselves. This was a language, you know, that we started ourselves.
Crook, [Harmon,] Hewlin and I, you wouldn't know what we were talking about, right now.
We could start the conversation -- the three of us, you know, and we could talk here for 15 or 20 minutes and you wouldn't know what we were talking about.
I think I was the instigator of that thing.
Yeah, he more or less started it, you know.
Baby, you were the instigator of this new language; all right, now this is one band, okay, so you had your own thing. Do you think other bands did the same thing?
Definitely, definitely.
Oh yeah.
See, I remember in the early '30s I run into --
Oh, excuse me, Crook, I'm going to interrupt. Would that be one -- when you say bands, are you talking about just black bands or white bands?
I think they all do it.
Okay.
I think they all do it, both black and white because you have a certain bound there where you're not selfish now, it's not that. It's you just want to talk and you don't want --
It was like a club --
Yeah.
-- a private, a secret society?

Yeah, just like in the early '30s, you know, you take a lot of people now, they speak of being hip. Well this goes back to that, you know. I remember when they had what we called the hip dictionary, you know. Well, you know, just like you saying "the phone". You wouldn't say the phone, you'd say the grapevine, okay, you know. They had different names for different things.
